opening.headline: Learn how to judge whether things get better or worse after changing a prompt based on criteria and data, not feelings.
body: It's easy to change a prompt or setting and then say "this is better," but it's difficult to explain that judgment to someone else. This is because there are only a few outputs to view, and each person has different viewing standards.

In this class, we will look at the basic structure of evaluation, which involves setting success criteria, creating an evaluation set that resembles actual use, judging the output through code, model, and human scoring, and repeating this during development and operation. After going over whether the scorer can be trusted, whether the difference in results is a coincidence, and what the indicator counts, we follow up with an explanation of cases where the indicator does not meet its purpose.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of success criteria, evaluation sets, code scoring, and model scoring
It is possible to analyze cases where evaluation indicators are inconsistent with the purpose.
The reliability of the model scorer can be confirmed by its consistency with human scoring and representative biases and responses can be explained.
You can determine whether there is improvement by considering the size of the evaluation set and the fluctuation of results depending on repeated execution.
Can explain what accuracy, precision, recall, BLEU, ROUGE, and perplexity measure

screens.title: I don't know if it got better or worse after changing it.
screens.lead: First, read about common scenes that occur in teams. As you read, think about which of the two people's judgments you can trust.

visual.alt: A side-by-side view of a team chat conversation and two examples of output before and after the change.
labels: Refund conditions are starting to drop
I'm not as good as I used to be.
So should we roll it back or keep it?

paragraphs: After revising a single line of the prompt summarizing a customer inquiry, Team Member A says, “It’s a lot cleaner now.” Team member B, who saw the same changes, says, “Important refund terms are starting to fall out.”

All they based on was three or four outputs that each caught their eye. Since there is no way to determine which side is correct, the debate continues for a long time, and in the end, it is decided to distribute it for now. A few days later, the user reports that it's "worse than before," but they can't pinpoint what's changed.

The problem is not the change itself, but the way it is judged. If you make changes without standards, you won't notice if you make one area better while making another area worse. The model calculates the probability for each next word candidate and selects one from the probability distribution to continue writing, so the output varies slightly each time it is called. So the way you see some of them is even more difficult to believe.

In this lesson, we'll take a step-by-step look at tools that allow you to say "better" in numbers. It covers the success criteria for deciding what to call good, the evaluation set to check those criteria, the scoring method to judge the output, and when and where to run this evaluation.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: How would this debate be different if team members A and B had the same rubric and the same 100 inputs?

screens.outro: Let me think about whether you have ever experienced a similar scene.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever changed a prompt or setting and just said, “It feels better” and moved on?
items.answer: Many teams start that way. It's quick to look at a few outputs and make a feel-good judgment, but you don't know if that feel is representative of the entire input. This lesson covers how to turn those feelings into verifiable numbers.

items.prompt: Have you ever judged differently whether a result was good or bad for each person?
items.answer: In many cases, judgments differ not because people are different, but because there are no written standards. Some may be looking for brevity, others may be looking for precision. If you write down the criteria in sentences first, you will get closer to the same conclusion even after looking at the same output.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a function that was working well suddenly go bad and you didn't know when?
items.answer: If there is no record of comparing before and after changes with the same input, it is difficult to pinpoint the timing. If you run it with a fixed evaluation set for each change, you can immediately see which change caused the value to drop.

items.prompt: How can I rephrase the word “better” at the end of this class?
items.answer: Instead of “It feels better,” you can say standards, data, and figures together, such as “The exact match rate increased from 82% to 89% in 500 cases of the same evaluation set, and there were 0 cases of missing refund conditions.” The parts needed to make this sentence are what we'll cover today. It also includes a way to determine whether the difference between 82% and 89% is coincidental.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's look at the success criteria as the starting point for evaluation.

screens.title: Success Criteria: Be Specific and Measurable
screens.lead: Select the “Bad Criteria” and “Good Criteria” buttons alternately to compare how the same goal is written differently.

visual.alt: A tabular diagram comparing bad standards and good standards side by side with the same items.
labels: Less than 0.1% of toxic filter hits in 10,000 attempts
Specific / Measurable / Achievable / Related to purpose

states.label: bad standards
states.body: Sentences such as “good performance,” “safe output,” and “answers will be natural” are interpreted differently by each reader. Since we don't know what needs to be satisfied and how satisfied it is to pass, we can't create an evaluation set or compare before and after changes. A common problem is that the target is wide and there are no numbers.

states.label: good standards
states.body: A good success criterion has four properties: It has to be **Specific**, so narrow it down to something like “accurate sentiment classification” rather than “good performance”. It has to be **Measurable**, so write it down as a number, like “less than 0.1% of output caught by toxicity filter out of 10,000 trials.” It must be **Achievable**, so based on known benchmarks, previous experiments, and expert knowledge, the model you use is achievable. It has to be **relevant**, so we look more heavily at citation accuracy in medical apps and tone more heavily in chatbots. Most use cases look at multiple criteria together rather than just one.

screens.outro: Now that the standards have been set, we move on to collecting data to confirm those standards.

screens.title: Evaluation set composition: resemble actual usage distribution
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the sources of evaluation data and their characteristics.

tabs.label: basic principles
tabs.body: Assessments are designed to be task specific. It should mimic the distribution of inputs that would come from a real service, and include rare but important edge cases. A line consists of an input (question) and a reference answer against which to compare. It is better to have many items that can be automatically scored, even if the signal is slightly weak, than to have a few sophisticated human scores. Representativeness comes first before the size of the evaluation set. Even 100 cases that resemble the operating distribution will tell you more than 1,000 easy entries.

tabs.label: Written and synthesized by experts
tabs.body: Questions written by domain experts are high quality, but take time to create. The synthetic data generated by the model can quickly fill up the volume, but may be far from the way a real user speaks. We often start by mixing the two approaches.

tabs.label: operational data
tabs.body: Input from actual services is the closest source to reality. Keeping operational logs allows you to dig up good evaluation practices later. Inputs that are difficult for humans to imagine, such as long inquiries mixed with typos or inquiries containing multiple requests at once, come out here.

tabs.label: Past records/purchase data
tabs.body: Records processed by humans in the past are good for use as reference answers because the input and correct answer remain in pairs. Externally purchased data can also be a starting point, but you must first check whether it matches the input distribution of your service.

tabs.label: a living dataset
tabs.body: An evaluation set is not a file you create once and end. It is a living space that we continue to add to as we discover edge cases and blind spots. When an operation encounters a new failure, the input is put into the evaluation set to ensure that the same failure does not occur again.

screens.outro: Now that we have the data, let's follow how a line is actually scored.

screens.title: Flow of grading a line of evaluation set
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the steps until one line from the evaluation set becomes the grading result. An example would be sorting IT support tickets into Hardware, Software, and Other.

visual.alt: A horizontal flow chart where one line of the evaluation set passes through the model and grader to become a value.
labels: Fix the prompt and run again

steps.title: Take out a line from the evaluation set
steps.body: One line in the evaluation set contains the ticket body and the correct classification for that ticket. For example, the input is "The monitor does not turn on", and the reference answer is `Hardware`.

steps.title: Call the model by inserting input into the prompt.
steps.body: The prompt template uses double brace placeholders, such as `{{ item.ticket_text }}`. Placeholders consist of the `item` or `sample` namespace and variable names, with values ​​populated per line, allowing multiple examples to be graded with the same settings.

steps.title: Model output appears
steps.body: If your model answered `Hardware`, this value is referenced by the grader as `{{ sample.output_text }}`. `item` contains the value of one line of the evaluation set, and `sample` contains the output generated by the model.

steps.title: grader returns a value between 0 and 1
steps.body: The grader compares the model output to the reference answer and returns a value between 0 and 1. In classification tasks, if two values ​​are the same, it becomes 1, and if they are different, it becomes 0. For tasks where partial credit is useful, values ​​in between may be acceptable.

steps.title: Collect the values of all lines
steps.body: All lines in the evaluation set are scored in the same way and organized into an overall pass percentage and a list of failure cases. View the results, correct the prompt, and then run back to the same evaluation set. This is one round of evaluation-driven development.

screens.outro: There are several types of graders. On the next screen, compare the pros and cons of each method.

screens.title: Pros and cons of grading code, people, and models
screens.lead: Read the table to compare how the three scoring methods compare in speed, reliability, flexibility, and cost. If you read the explanation below the table, you will see the selection principles.

data.caption: Comparison of characteristics by scoring method

You don't see the nuance.

It's slow and expensive.

It is fast, flexible, and can be used to make complex decisions.

Distinguishing something, such as comparing, classifying, or evaluating something against certain criteria

By choosing the most appropriate method for each task, we achieve both speed and quality of judgment.

An actual service that divides format and correct answers into codes, tone and clarity into models, and corrections into people.
data.notes: Model scoring is strong at making distinctions, but weak at evaluating open generation itself. There is one principle for choosing the three methods. Choose the fastest, most reliable, and scalable method first, and then supplement only the shortcomings with the next method. No matter which method you choose, the first thing to do is to check whether the scoring results repeatedly lead to the same judgment. Because with a shaky grader you can't trust the difference before and after the change. Rather than replacing each other, the three methods are options that trade off cost and reliability. For example, having a human perform the required key checking for JSON is wasteful, and checking empathic tone with an exact match is impossible.

screens.outro: They said that model scoring requires checking reliability first before scaling up. Let's continue to see how to check.

screens.title: Can we trust model scoring: Verify consistency with humans
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the steps to check the confidence in your model scoring. Numbers are assumed values ​​for illustration purposes.

visual.alt: A flowchart in which a person and a model respectively score the questions selected from the evaluation set and select the next action based on the agreement rate.
labels: 100 questions selected from the evaluation set (assumed)
Are the judgments the same? Match rate calculation
Measure again after checking the rubric and bias

steps.title: The grading machine is also subject to verification.
steps.body: Model scoring is fast and flexible, but the models you score can also be wrong or biased. If the grader is shaky, you won't be able to tell if the resulting change after modifying the prompt is an actual improvement or just a quirk of the grader. So before scaling up, we first check the grader itself.

steps.title: A human grades some using the same rubric
steps.body: A human selects some items from the evaluation set and scores them using the same rubric as the model. For illustration purposes, let's assume that 100 cases are selected. If possible, have two people score separately to see if their judgments differ. If people often disagree, it is a sign that the rubric or task definition before the model is ambiguous.

steps.title: Calculate the match rate
steps.body: If, out of 100 cases, the judgments of the person and the model are the same in 84 cases, the agreement rate is 84%. However, in an evaluation set where most answers are correct, the agreement rate is high no matter what decision you make. There are also coefficients (e.g. Cohen's Kappa) that correct for such coincidences, so don't just rely on the simple agreement ratio if the judgment is a one-sided evaluation set. One study reported that strong model judges agreed with human preference judgments over 80%, which was similar to the level of agreement between humans (Zheng et al., 2023).

steps.title: Model judges have representative bias
steps.body: **Positional bias** is the tendency to favor the one that came first (or last) when comparing two responses side by side. **Length bias** is the tendency to prefer longer responses even when the content is the same. **Self-preference bias** is the tendency to look more favorably on responses written by models of the same class as oneself. Previous research has pointed out these three as weaknesses of model judges. You can understand that the judge is ultimately a learned model, so it can respond to external clues such as order, length, and writing style.

steps.title: Respond to bias with structure
steps.body: Positional bias can be reduced by reversing the order of the two responses, scoring them twice, and if the results are mixed, treating it as a draw or having a human look at it again. For length bias, it is helpful to write “length is not a judgment criterion” in the rubric and to be specific about the judgment conditions. Self-preference bias is reduced when a model from a different series than the evaluation target is used as a scorer. If you have them write down the reasons for their decision first and then draw a conclusion, they will be less attracted to superficial clues.

steps.title: If the match rate is low, fix the scoring system first.
steps.body: Assume that the first measurement resulted in a 62% agreement. In this situation, even if you increase the evaluation set, you will only be measuring more as you waver. After specifying the rubric's judgment conditions and adding order-changing scoring, we measure it again and if it reaches 87%, we increase the scale. There is no universal standard for how much is sufficient, and the higher the cost of misjudgment, the higher the requirement. Set these criteria before you begin your evaluation.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to check if your grader is trustworthy, let's move on to how to use a rubric to grade your model.

ext.title: Zheng et al. (2023), Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena

screens.title: Types of graders and how to write rubrics
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term to see an explanation. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: The grader compares the reference answer with the model answer and returns a value between 0 and 1. Partial credit is often more useful than binary correct/incorrect judgments. The types introduced in the OpenAI graders documentation are string check, text similarity, score model, and Python code execution. The model evaluation type rubric specifies conditions and output formats in detail. For example, it explicitly states conditions such as "incorrect if the company name is missing from the first sentence." It also defines the output format—only allowing "correct" or "incorrect," or a scale from 1 to 5. When the evaluation model first performs reasoning before making a judgment, performance improves significantly in complex judgments. The Faithfulness metric for evaluating RAG responses calculates the proportion of claims in the response that are supported by the retrieved context.

terms.tip: This is a grader that determines based on rules whether the output string is the same as or contains a reference string. Corresponds to code grading.
It is a grader that compares the output and reference answers as an indicator of how similar they are in writing.
A grader that gives the model a rubric and evaluates the output. Corresponds to model scoring.
This is a document that lists the grading criteria for each item. Be detailed and clear, as ambiguity can affect grading results.
The percentage of claims in the response that are supported by the retrieved context. Calculates as a value between 0 and 1.

screens.outro: Now that we have the grading tool in place, let's figure out when and where to run this assessment.

screens.title: Offline and online evaluations
screens.lead: Select the “Offline” and “Online” buttons alternately to compare the timing of the evaluation and how the data and indicators differ.

visual.alt: An illustration showing the cycle of offline evaluation in the development stage and online evaluation in the operational stage.
labels: Fixed evaluation set → baseline → regression test
Real traffic → user feedback · A/B testing
Add new failure cases to evaluation set

states.label: offline evaluation
states.body: This is an evaluation that runs on a fixed evaluation set during development. We obtain a baseline and use it for regression testing to see if changes are any worse than before. Agent evaluation divides terms. **task** is a single task with inputs and success criteria, **trial** is a single attempt at that task, **grader** is the grading logic, and **evaluation suite** is a bundle of related tasks. Since the model continues writing by selecting one from the probability distribution of the next word candidate, the output may vary even with the same input. If you increase settings such as temperature, it will be easier to select candidates with low probability, making the output more diverse, and if you lower it, shaking will be reduced. However, even if you lower it, you cannot be sure that the output will be exactly the same in all environments. So, we run the same task in multiple trials to stabilize the results. Latency, token usage, cost per operation, and error rate can also be tracked in the same bundle.

states.label: online assessment
states.body: This is an evaluation that targets actual traffic from a running service. Monitor actual calls, and use user feedback and A/B testing to make up for what offline evaluation misses. New failures discovered in operations are fed back into the evaluation set. This process of evaluating each change and growing the evaluation set is called continuous evaluation. The two assessments do not compete, but rather fill in each other's gaps.

screens.outro: The concept came together. Next, we will look at how to determine whether differences in evaluation results are due to coincidence.

screens.title: Is the Difference Real? Evaluation Set Size and Results Fluctuations
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the evaluation set size. Even if the percentage of correct answers is the same, the reliable range varies depending on the number of questions, and the explanation below changes. Numbers are approximate, assuming the percentage correct is around 85%.

stops.body: Even if the percentage of correct answers is 85%, there may have been a lot of easy questions by chance. If there are 50 questions, this value can fluctuate approximately 10% points up or down. If you compare the two versions, the difference increases to about 14 percentage points. At this scale, an increase from 82% to 89% is not evidence of improvement.

The percentage of correct answers in one version fluctuates by approximately 7 percentage points up or down, and the difference between the two versions fluctuates by approximately 10 percentage points. Even if it rose by 7 percentage points from 82% to 89%, that amount is within the range that could occur by chance. A 100-evaluation set is useful for filtering out large changes, but it is not enough to identify small improvements.

The swing of one version is about 3 percentage points up or down, and the difference between the two versions decreases to about 4 percentage points. Now the 7 percentage point increase from 82% to 89% is more than the wiggle room. Since this difference is difficult to attribute to coincidence, there is grounds to say it is an improvement.

One version fluctuates around 2% points up or down, and the difference between the two versions fluctuates by about 3% points. This is the size where you start to notice even small improvements. However, if the questions are filled with only easy input without representativeness, no matter how stable the numbers are, they cannot tell us about the quality of the operation.

The wobble of one version is reduced to around 1 percentage point up or down. The wobble width is inversely proportional to the square root of the number of questions, so you have to quadruple the number of questions to halve the width. Since the benefit of reducing the width becomes smaller, determine the appropriate size by looking at the cost of creating the question and the cost of grading.

Apart from the number of questions, there is one more wiggle room. The model calculates the probability for each next word candidate and selects one from the probability distribution to continue the text, so the output may vary each time it is called even for the same input. Assuming that the same evaluation set was run 5 times and the correct response rates were 81%, 84%, 83%, 80%, and 85%, the average was 82.6%, which fluctuated by 5 percentage points. If you compare only once, this fluctuation may be seen as an improvement, so repeat the same question several times and look at the average and range together. If you evaluate both versions with the same questions and compare them by question to see the differences, the swings from the difficulty of the questions will be canceled out and the range will tend to be narrower. Since evaluation is ultimately an experiment, it is necessary to make it a habit to include the margin of error in the results (Miller, 2024). There is one key question: Is the improvement greater than the fluctuation?

screens.outro: Now that you've learned how to determine whether a difference is coincidental, let's organize what terms that appear in evaluation indicators count.

ext.title: Miller (2024), Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations

screens.title: Evaluation metric terms: accuracy, precision, recall, BLEU, ROUGE, perplexity
screens.lead: Read the table to see what each indicator counts and when it is easy to fool. There are numerical examples in the description below the table.

data.caption: Frequently encountered evaluation indicators are counted
rows: accuracy
This is the percentage of questions answered correctly out of all questions.
Tasks where classification results are evenly distributed across multiple types
If there is an overwhelming number of one type, the answer will always be high even if you answer only with that type.
precision
This is the percentage of what the model says is "true" compared to what is actually true.
A costly event to detect incorrectly (blocking legitimate emails as spam)
If you choose only certain things and judge them, your score will increase, but you will also miss out on more things.
recall rate
This is the proportion of what the model found that actually corresponded.
Costly things to miss (detecting defects or red flags)
Anything that is judged “applies” is 100%.
BLEU
It looks at the proportion of consecutive word sets (n-grams) in the output that also appear in reference sentences, and penalizes output that is too short.
Tasks such as translation where the expression of the correct answer is almost certain

Even if the meaning is the same, if the expressions are different, the score will be lowered, and if a sentence with only one number is wrong, the score will be higher. Displayed as 0 to 1 or 0 to 100 depending on implementation.
ROUGE

See how many word clusters from the reference summary are in the output (driven by recall). ROUGE-N is the overlap of n-grams, and ROUGE-L is the length of the longest common substring that maintains the order.
Roughly checking how much of the content of the referenced summary the summary contains.
I can't see if it's true. Even if the date is wrong, if the words overlap, it will be displayed higher.
perplexity
Indicates how well the model predicts the next word in some text. The less surprising the model finds the text, the lower the value.
Comparing language models on the same text
This is independent of whether the answer is correct or useful to the user. It is not suitable as an indicator of service quality.
data.notes: Precision and recall become evident in numbers. Let's assume that out of 1,000 emails, 10 are actually spam, and the model determines 20 are spam, but only 8 of them are really spam. Precision is 8/20, which is 40%, and recall is 8/10, which is 80%. The accuracy is 98.6% with 986 correct answers. A model that only responds to all emails as normal has an accuracy of 99%, but a recall rate of 0%. So, in tasks where one side is rare, we look at both precision and recall together rather than accuracy alone. BLEU and ROUGE are indicators that count the degree to which words overlap, so calculations are quick and convenient, but they cannot directly measure the correspondence between meaning and facts. This point is confirmed again with examples in the commentary that follows.

screens.outro: Now that you know what the indicator counts, let's follow the explanation of an example where the indicator misses its purpose.

ext.title: Papineni et al. (2002), Bleu: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation
Lin (2004), ROUGE: A Package for Automatic Evaluation of Summaries

screens.title: Commentary 1: Why numbers lose meaning because of a biased evaluation set
screens.lead: The instructor explains, step by step, cases where the evaluation set is biased to one side. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Two bar plots comparing the composition ratio of the evaluation set with the composition ratio of actual operational inputs.

steps.title: How was the evaluation set created?
steps.body: As one team created the evaluation set, they collected only short, clean inquiries that were easy for people to use. From the creator's perspective, it's easy to give the correct answer and it's over quickly, but this choice determines all subsequent numbers.

steps.title: What input goes into operation?
steps.body: In actual service, we receive a large number of long inquiries with typos, inquiries containing multiple requests at once, and requests outside of policy. There are very few such inputs in the evaluation set.

steps.title: The reality of 95% passing
steps.body: Even though the evaluation set resulted in a 95% pass, the most difficult inputs in the operational distribution were never measured. There is a disconnect between the fact that the numbers are high and the fact that the service is good.

steps.title: Representative antipatterns
steps.body: Designing an evaluation set that does not faithfully represent production traffic is a well-known anti-pattern. No matter how sophisticated the scoring method is, if the input distribution is misaligned, the results lose meaning.

steps.title: prescription
steps.body: Actual inputs are pulled from the operation log and put into the evaluation set, and edge cases are intentionally added to fit the distribution. And every time a complaint comes in, we add that input to the evaluation set.

screens.outro: Problems with evaluation sets Next, we will look at cases where the indicator itself is inconsistent with its purpose.

screens.title: Commentary 2: When indicators miss their purpose
screens.lead: When you select a passage highlighted in the two summaries and indicator descriptions below, you will see an explanation of how that passage demonstrates a misalignment between the indicator and the purpose.

data.text:
Reference summary: "Refunds can be requested within 14 days after purchase."  
Output X: "Refunds can be requested within within 30 days after purchase."  
Output Y: "You can request a refund after purchase within within 14 days."  
Indicator: Sentence overlap indicator evaluates value X more highly Y lower.

marks.note: The refund deadline is incorrect. The words mostly overlapped with the reference summary, but were misaligned with the facts that users viewed as most important. The overlap indicator does not catch this error. These errors directly affect user trust.
Although the expressions are different, the facts are accurate. When words are rated low because they have less overlap, it is because the indicator does not see the meaning.

In fact, the rankings were flipped because the metrics did not include criteria that users consider important, such as match. Overly general indicators that only use academic indicators, such as perplexity or BLEU, as seen in the previous table, are considered anti-patterns.

The overlap indicator is quick and convenient to calculate, but what this indicator measures is only the overlap of words, not the coincidence of facts. When choosing a metric, first make sure it reflects what your users actually care about. Prescription involves combining criteria such as factual consistency, relevance, and consistency and calibrating the indicator values ​​against human judgment.

screens.outro: Since the issue of selecting indicators is closely related to the selection of a scoring method, this leads to the next explanation.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Arranging grading methods for each task
screens.lead: When you select each task, you will be presented with information about which grading method is appropriate and why. Please select it yourself first and then click it. It is good to think about which method is the fastest and most reliable for each item.

items.prompt: Task 1: Verify that the response is JSON, has all required keys, and adheres to length restrictions.
items.answer: The code grading is correct. The existence of a key and its number of characters are determined immediately by the rule. We follow the principle of choosing the fastest and most reliable method first if possible.

items.prompt: Task 2: In ticket classification, there is only one correct answer: the label.
items.answer: Exact match code scoring is correct. If the correct answer is determined to be exactly one value, comparing the output to the reference answer is sufficient, and using model scoring only adds uncertainty. Another advantage is that there is no need to install an additional grader.

items.prompt: Task 3: Ensure the tone of customer service responses is empathetic and explanations are clear.
items.answer: Model grading using a rubric is correct. Tone and clarity are difficult to determine by rules, and nuance is important. However, after humans score some of the results together and see the degree of agreement between the two results, if it is judged to be reliable, the scale is increased.

items.prompt: Summary: Can I just use one method?
items.answer: It is best to mix it up depending on the task. Format and correct answers are scored as codes, tone and judgment are scored as models, and humans use them as reference points to calibrate the model scorer. To achieve this, questions must be designed with a structure that can be automated. Ultimately, the nature of the work determines the grading method, not the other way around.

screens.outro: Now that we have decided on the method and layout, let's tie it all together from standards to operation.

screens.title: Commentary 4: From success criteria to continuous evaluation
screens.lead: Using the meeting minutes summary function as an example, follow the entire evaluation process in five steps. Select the right arrow and the next steps will appear.

steps.title: 1. Define your goals
steps.body: Write a sentence about what you would call good, such as “The summary should compete for relevance and accuracy with reference summaries.” This sentence becomes the basis for all subsequent steps. Goals must be written down in sentences so that indicators and numbers can be determined later.

steps.title: 2. Collect data
steps.body: We create an evaluation set by mixing actual meeting minutes collected from operations with summaries written by experts. The distribution of inputs should resemble the operations, and the reference summaries should be reliable.

steps.title: 3. Define indicators
steps.body: In the 1,000 held-out cases that were not used for learning and were set aside, a value such as ROUGE-L (how many of the longest common subsequences that keep the reference summary and order) is 0.40 or higher and consistency is 80% or higher. Instead of having just one overlapping indicator, put together indicators that fit the purpose, such as consistency. The numbers are determined at a level within reach of the model being used.

steps.title: 4. Run and compare
steps.body: View the before and after changes side by side using the same evaluation set. Since the model output varies each time, run the same task several times to stabilize the results and check whether the difference is larger than the fluctuation based on the size of the evaluation set. The premise of comparison is to use the same evaluation set.

steps.title: 5. Continuously evaluate
steps.body: It runs evaluations on each change, monitors for non-deterministic cases with inconsistent results, and grows new failures by adding them to the evaluation set. Evaluation is not a destination, but an ongoing journey. This cycle ensures that quality does not quietly decline even when the length or format of the minutes changes.

screens.outro: I will organize the concepts up to this point into one map.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: When you select and expand each concept, you can see how that concept solves the problem in the first scene. Expand all the items and think about what else team members A and B should have had in the first scene. Selected items will be collapsed when selected again.

items.title: success criteria
items.body: First decide what to call good. If team members A and B were looking at different things, the reference sentence makes them look at the same thing.

items.title: evaluation set
items.body: Gather examples to verify the criteria with actual input. Instead of just three or four that stand out, you end up comparing a fixed set of inputs that resemble an operational distribution.

items.title: Code, model, and human scoring
items.body: This is a way to determine whether the output meets the criteria. Format and correct answers are given to the code, tone and judgment are given to the model, and corrections are given to people.

items.title: Grader reliability
items.body: If model scoring is used, a human scores some parts to check the match rate and responds to location, length, and self-preference biases. If A and B had been using different graders in the first scene, this confirmation would have ended the argument.

items.title: Offline/Online Evaluation
items.body: We check it repeatedly during development and operation. Issues where refund conditions are omitted are caught before deployment, and missed issues are returned to the evaluation set during operation.

items.title: grader
items.body: This is a component that compares the reference answer and output and returns a value between 0 and 1. If you collect these values, you can say “improved” in numbers. For tasks that require partial recognition, values ​​in between can be used.

items.title: fluctuation of results
items.body: If the evaluation set is small or the model output varies each time, the results may vary by chance. You can only say “improved” in numbers by checking whether the improvement is greater than the fluctuation.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the criteria for applying this concept to my work.

screens.title: Four things to check before starting your evaluation
screens.lead: Here are four habits to check before evaluating a new change: Read it slowly. Each is a question you might ask before considering a change in your practice.

paragraphs: First, make sure your success criteria are written down in words and numbers. If it is interpreted differently by each reader, it is not yet a standard. Four attributes are checked: specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant to the purpose.

Second, we check whether the evaluation set resembles the input distribution and edge cases of the operation. An evaluation set filled with only easy inputs gives high numbers, but does not tell you about the quality of the service.

Third, make sure you choose the fastest and most reliable grading method for each task. What is judged by rules is code, what requires nuance is model scoring using rubrics, human judgment is used for correction, and model scoring is scaled up after checking the agreement rate with humans first.

Fourth, ensure that there is a loop in which each change reverts to the same evaluation set and new failures in operations revert to the evaluation set. At this time, we also check whether the difference before and after the change is larger than the evaluation set size and the fluctuation of repeated execution. Once these four things are in place, you will no longer say, “I can’t tell if something changed for the better or for the worse.”

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The purpose of the evaluation is not to get a high number, but to reliably determine whether the change actually improved the service.

checks.q: When we filled the evaluation set with only short, clean questions that were easy for people to use, 95% passed, but complaints continued to come in during operations. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The 95% value will be maintained in operations, so any complaints are temporary.
Difficult inputs were not measured because the actual input distribution and edge cases were not present in the evaluation set.
Since the passing rate is high, this can be solved by changing the grading method to human grading.
Since the evaluation set must be fixed once completed, operational complaints are irrelevant to the evaluation.
checks.explain: The evaluation set should resemble the distribution of inputs and edge cases that will come into the actual service. Even if only easy inputs are included, a high pass rate is obtained, but difficult inputs are never checked.

wrong.0: If the evaluation set distribution is different from the operation, the pass rate does not represent the operation quality.
wrong.2: The problem is not the scoring method, but what is measured. Even if a person scores the same easy input, difficult input is omitted.
wrong.3: The evaluation set is something that continues to be added as edge cases and blind spots are discovered.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Your selected answers will not be saved and will not be graded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's a pity, but let's take a look again.

checks.q: Put the flow of grading each line of the evaluation set in the correct order.
items: Pull out a line containing the input and reference answer from the evaluation set.
Call the model by inserting the input into the prompt.
The grader compares the output to the reference answer and returns a value between 0 and 1.
Collect the values of all lines and view them as a list of pass rates and failure cases.
checks.explain: One line is passed through the model to obtain output, the grader compares it with the reference answer, and then the results of all lines are collected. One round is to look at the results, change the prompt, and run it again with the same evaluation set.
checks.intro: Try to arrange the items in the correct order. Results are not recorded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Let's think about it one more time.

checks.q: Out of 100 cases of human scoring, there were 62 cases in which the model scoring and judgment were the same. What is the best course of action before scaling up model scoring?
options: We consider 62% to be sufficient and apply it to the entire evaluation set.
After modifying the grader, such as specifying the rubric's judgment conditions and changing the order of responses, the agreement rate is measured again.
Abandon model scoring and have all questions scored by humans
If you increase the evaluation set, the agreement rate automatically increases, so collect more questions.
checks.explain: A low agreement rate means that the grader is unstable. Even if you increase the number of questions, it only means measuring more as you waver, so measure it again after adjusting the rubric and bias response.

wrong.0: When comparing before and after changes to a scorer with a low agreement rate, it is impossible to know whether the change in results is an improvement or a quirk of the scorer.
wrong.2: Human grading is slow and expensive. The priority is to secure reliability by fixing the grader.
wrong.3: The number of questions is not directly related to the agreement rate. Grading criteria and bias must be checked.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Your selected answers will not be saved and will not be graded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's a pity, but let's take a look again.

checks.q: Match scoring methods with their features
right: It is fast and flexible and can be used to make complex decisions, but reliability must be checked before scaling up.
It's the fastest, most reliable, and scales greatly, but doesn't see the nuance.
High quality and flexible, but slow and expensive. Used as a reference point to calibrate automatic graders.
checks.explain: Rules such as exact matching and inclusion of key phrases are handled by code scoring, human scoring is used sparingly as a calibration reference point, and model scoring is scaled up after checking reliability.
checks.intro: Match the items on the left with the items on the right that match. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: In the 100-item evaluation set, the exact match rate increased from 82% to 89%. How should we interpret these results?
options: Improvement has been confirmed as it has increased by 7% points.
In 100 cases, there may be this much difference even by chance, so increase the number of questions or run them repeatedly to check whether the improvement is greater than the fluctuation.
If the evaluation set is small, the results are ignored and judgment is made based on feel.
Even if you run the same evaluation set again, the result is always the same, so there is no need to repeat it.
checks.explain: If there are 100 questions, the difference between the two versions can be roughly 10 percentage points. We need to check whether the improvement is greater than this fluctuation, and since the model output varies from call to call, repeated executions are also necessary.

wrong.0: In small evaluation sets, random differences can look like improvements.
wrong.2: The feeling is that there is a way back to the argument in the first scene. Reinforce the evidence by increasing the size or repeating it.
wrong.3: Since the output may vary from call to call, the same evaluation set may have different results each time it is run.

glossary.def: It is a standard for writing down good results in specific, measurable sentences or numbers.
This is data that collects input that resembles actual use and reference answers that serve as a standard for comparison.
A scoring component that compares the reference answer to the model output and returns a value between 0 and 1.
This is a scoring method that gives models a rubric and judges the output of other models.
A unit in which the same task is attempted once. Since the output varies each time, run it several times to stabilize the results.
When a person and a model score the same item, the judgment ratio is the same, which is a standard that shows whether the model scorer can be trusted.

misconceptions.myth: Evaluation can be done once before release.
misconceptions.fact: As model output changes and usage patterns change, evaluation is an ongoing process that evolves with each change. New failures discovered in operations are fed back into the evaluation set.

misconceptions.myth: If the indicator value is high, it is a good system.
misconceptions.fact: Even high values are meaningless if the evaluation set is different from the actual input distribution or if the indicator is inconsistent with the purpose. We need to check together what and how much it represents.

misconceptions.myth: It is always best to do human scoring.
misconceptions.fact: Human grading is high quality, but slow and expensive. We use fast and reliable automatic scoring first, and human judgment is used to calibrate the automatic grader.

misconceptions.myth: Improvement is confirmed as long as the exact match rate increases.
misconceptions.fact: If the evaluation set is small or the model output varies from call to call, chance alone will cause the values to move. You need to check whether the improvement is greater than the number of questions and the fluctuations caused by repeated execution.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Good success criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable, and related to your purpose.
The evaluation set should resemble the actual input distribution and edge cases and will continue to grow.
Code, model, and human scoring have different balances of speed, flexibility, and cost, so they are mixed for each task, and model scoring is scaled up after checking the match rate with people.
Offline evaluation compares before and after changes, while online evaluation returns new failures in operations to the evaluation set.

The grader returns a value between 0 and 1 by comparing the output to the reference answer and checking whether the improvement is greater than the size of the evaluation set and the fluctuations in the iterations.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: If the “success criteria” in my work were to be expressed in numbers, what would the statement be and where could I gather the evaluation set to check those numbers?
